# Paint

> A local-first sketchpad PWA: draw a concept on a canvas, switch extra tools on
> when you need them, and keep every drawing on your device — with optional
> Dropbox or Google Drive sync.

Paint is a small, installable web app for sketching the kind of diagram you draw
to explain something: boxes, arrows, a circled bit, a scribble. Drawings are
vector strokes stored as JSON in your browser; nothing is uploaded unless you
connect a storage backend yourself.

## What it does

- Draw with a pen, a marker, a highlighter, an airbrush, an eraser, a paint
  bucket (and the gradient behind it, which fills the same
  area with a ramp of its own colours), the shapes, a selection marquee, a text
  tool and a colour dropper, plus a hand tool that drags the page around — the
  toolbar out of the box.
- Set every tool in the sizes it is really made in. A page pixel is one dot of
  an iPhone's screen, so widths are millimetres you can measure on the glass at
  1:1: the pencil offers the
  four leads a mechanical pencil takes, the paintbrush a #2 round through a
  one-inch flat, type is set in points, and each tool's slider spends its
  middle four tenths on the range that tool is genuinely manufactured in.
- Reach for a tool the way its medium is actually used: every tool ships with a
  row of presets — the pencil as Sketch, Construction, Shading and Detail, the
  watercolour brush as a wash, wet-in-wet, a glaze and a dry brush, the
  calligraphy pen as an italic, foundational or uncial hand — and each chip sets
  a width and every dial at once, showing the mark it makes.
- Paint a wash with a pigment simulation: water and colour go onto the paper a
  step at a time and the mark is whatever dries — blooms, backruns, a frayed wet
  edge, granulation that rolls into the paper's valleys, and a rim that gathers
  where the wash actually stopped. A detail slider in the brush's own panel
  trades fineness for speed, and a browser that cannot run the field at all still
  paints the wash.
- Draw with a pencil that presses a lead into the page's own paper and draws
  whatever the sheet kept — a hard lead riding the peaks and leaving the valleys
  bare, a second pass filling in what the first could not reach, a black it
  cannot go past however long you shade, and the crowns of a canvas weave
  catching while the troughs skip. The page's surface and grain dial decide all
  of it, along with a pressure dial for how hard the hand is bearing down —
  light rides the crowns, heavy fills the tooth in. A detail slider in the pencil's own panel trades fineness for speed, and
  a browser that cannot run it still draws the line.
- Choose what the page is made of when the drawing is made, alongside its size:
  a solid digital sheet, four papers (cartridge, cold-pressed, rough,
  hot-pressed) or primed cotton duck. The sheet stays with the drawing and cannot
  be swapped afterwards, because a mark is painted into the sheet it was made
  on. Its grain is painted under the marks, and how wet a tool is times how
  thirsty the sheet is decides whether a mark covers what it is over or mixes
  into it, how far its water runs past the nib, and how much of an ink line it
  crosses it drags out into the wash. Wet mixing is scoped to one layer.
- Save a tool you have set up under a name — "my sketching pencil" — and get
  its width and every dial back in one press.
- Draw eleven shapes from one toolbar button: rectangle, ellipse, line, arrow,
  rounded rectangle, triangle, diamond, pentagon, hexagon, star and double
  arrow. Press the button a second time for the family and the fill toggle.
- Cut a window in the page with the selection tools: draw a box, an oval or a
  freehand lasso over what you drew, trace the contours of what is already
  painted, or paint the selection in with a pencil-like nib that adds with every
  stroke, erases with a mode flip or a held Ctrl, and feathers what a Delete
  takes out — five gestures behind one button, pressed a second time to choose.
  Invert the window — or delete the traced subject's background — from the
  side panel's Contextual block, which is there only while a selection is.
  What settles is an area, not a list of marks: paint in it and the mark is cut
  to it, drag it with the hand to carry what is painted under it, drag it with
  the marquee to slide the window itself, and pull its corner grips to adjust it
  under a 300% magnifier. Delete (or a tap with the rubber) clears what is
  inside; copy, cut and paste work from the keyboard, a right-click or a long
  press. Ctrl/Cmd+V pastes marks, a picture or words back
  into the drawing — words open the caption box so the typeface and size are
  yours to set first.
- Press the eraser a second time for the rubber behind it: it lifts pencil and chalk the
  way a real one does — a little at a time, never all of it, and never the ink,
  paint or crayon laid beside it.
- Switch more tools on in Settings → Tools (a graphite pencil, a watercolour
  brush that spreads and granulates, a bristle paintbrush that runs
  from a round to a one-stroke flat on a dial and simulates a finite dip of
  paint over the page's grain, a wax crayon that runs from china marker to
  oil pastel, a board chalk that sparkles and dusts past its own edge,
  calligraphy pen),
  and put the rows in the order you want
  the toolbar in. Every tool is a plugin behind one interface, so the list grows
  without the app changing shape.
- Type on the page: the text tool opens a caret where you tap, in four
  typefaces, five type sizes, bold and italic. Drag the caption box to reposition
  it before you keep it.
- Pick colour and stroke width from two buttons: a palette with a free colour
  mixer that remembers what you mix, and a nib picker with your own widths. Every
  width is shown as a real press with the tool in your hand — the mark it would
  leave, on your page, in your ink — rather than as a dot. The width is
  remembered per tool, and each tool opens at a width of its own. Widths read in
  millimetres of page, from a technical pen's 0.5 to a decorator's 200.
- Tune the tool in your hand under the nib picker's Advanced fold — how charged
  the head is, how much paint the dip took, how far the head is squeezed toward
  a flat, which way the blade is turned and how hard the hand is bearing on it
  for the paintbrush, flow for the
  airbrush, softness and pressure for the crayon, pressure for the chalk, the
  lead's grade and the hand on it for the pencil, the chisel of a felt tip and which way it
  is turned for the marker and the highlighter, the nib's angle and its dip of
  ink for the calligraphy pen, strength for the eraser,
  pressure for the rubber, a feathered edge for the paint bucket and the
  gradient, how much page one press of the dropper reads, opacity for the pen,
  the felt tips, the shapes and type. The simulated media carry no opacity —
  each is lightened the way that medium is, by the hand, the pigment or the
  dip. Each tool keeps its own settings — including the inks a tool mixes
  for itself, like the gradient's two ends and its optional middle — and a mark
  remembers what it was drawn with. On a desktop the pointer is drawn as the nib
  itself: a circle the size of the mark, at the page's own scale.
- Start a drawing from an empty page, an image file, or an image on the
  clipboard. An empty one asks its canvas size up front — this screen, Full HD,
  4K, A4 or a size you type, drawn to one shared scale so they can be compared
  at a glance. Every size stands the way the screen is being held, so a phone
  offers four upright pages, and one Flip turns the whole shelf over.
- Set a page up once and name it — a canvas preset, standing on that shelf beside
  the shipped sizes. A preset carries a size, optionally the sheet it is usually
  on (which lands in the picker as a suggestion), and optionally its own toolbar:
  the tools that page is worked with, in the order they sit in, put back every
  time a drawing made on it is opened. Each of those tools can be set up as well
  — which member of a family the page's button opens on, and the width and dials
  it opens at, so a sketchbook page comes back with a kneaded rubber rather than
  just an eraser. Settings → Canvas makes them, and hides any shipped size you
  never reach for.
- Resize, flip (a quarter turn either way) and mirror a whole drawing from the
  right-hand panel; resizing can scale the drawing or change only the sheet,
  which is how a page is cropped or given more room. The resize dialog draws the
  new page over the old one and lets it be pulled by its corners, crop-tool
  style, with a latch that keeps the proportions. The same panel's bin starts
  the drawing over — every mark, every layer and the page colour.
- Crop a drawing by eye: Crop… in the same panel puts a rectangle over the page
  with everything it would cut away dimmed, draggable by any edge, any corner or
  from the middle. A small card at the foot of the canvas locks the shape — keep
  the page's own proportions, drag freely, pick 1:1, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9 or 9:16, or
  type two numbers of your own — and Enter (or Crop) cuts the sheet down to the
  rectangle. Marks that fall outside it are kept in the document rather than
  deleted, so undo, or a bigger page later, brings them back.
- Blur or scatter grain from the right-hand panel's Effects section, with the
  radius, the amount, the speck size and coloured-or-grey grain set in the
  effect's own dialog. An effect is applied once and is then part of the picture:
  it rasterises the layers it lands on into an image with the effect in them, so
  marks made afterwards are unaffected, blurring twice blurs the blur, and
  drawing or rubbing out on what you softened costs nothing extra. Noise applies
  to the selected layer; blur applies to that layer or to every showing, unlocked
  layer, each one baked on its own so the stack survives. The page behind shows
  the effect as the sliders move and nothing lands until Apply; undo puts the
  marks back. Every download carries it without special handling.
- Draw on a page bigger than the window: the canvas is a window onto it, with
  pinch-to-zoom, two-finger panning, and one-finger panning under the hand. Zoom
  reaches sixteen screen pixels to the document pixel, and once a pixel is about
  five of them wide the page rules itself into single pixels — the squares a
  downloaded image resolves to. That threshold is an apparent size rather than a
  percentage, so it lands around 500% on a desktop screen and nearer 1500% on a
  phone, where a pixel is physically smaller; either way the squares are big
  enough to see when the grid arrives. Like the optional guide grid it is painted
  on the screen only and never reaches a downloaded file; Settings turns it off.
- Zoom out on a big drawing: only the part of the page on screen is painted, so
  the picture fills in when the gesture ends. Settings → Performance → "render
  the whole picture" keeps the whole drawing painted off to one side instead, at
  the cost of a page-sized image in memory and a background repaint after every
  change, and a zoom out then reveals it as it goes. Off out of the box on every
  device.
- Adjust the colour from the right-hand panel's Colour section: brightness and
  contrast, levels (black point, white point, midtones), curves (a draggable tone
  curve with a composite RGB line and one per channel), hue and saturation,
  colour balance aimed at the shadows, midtones or highlights with an optional
  keep-the-light switch, and desaturate. Each is an effect like blur and grain —
  the page behind previews it as the controls move, nothing lands until Apply,
  it applies to the selected layer or to every showing, unlocked layer, and it
  rasterises what it lands on so marks made afterwards are unaffected. Undo puts
  the marks back. The page colour is not a mark and is never changed.
- Delete a picture's background from the panel's Image section: trace roughly
  over the subject with a selection tool and the cut finds the subject's exact
  edge near the outline — everything well inside the tracing is kept, everything
  well outside goes, and the strip between is searched for the strongest
  continuous colour border. Feather, colour tolerance and smoothness are set in
  the effect's dialog, the page behind previews the cut, and it bakes the layer
  like every effect: applied once, undo puts the marks back, and it runs
  entirely on the device.

- Stack a drawing into layers: swipe in from the right edge of the canvas (or
  use the header button) for a panel that adds, selects, shows, hides, locks,
  reorders, merges and deletes them, each row previewing the marks on that
  layer. Every drawing starts with a locked Background layer — which carries the
  page colour, stays at the bottom of the stack and takes nothing underneath it,
  and is switched off on a page made with no colour — and one layer above it.
  New marks land on the selected layer; a hidden layer leaves the screen and
  every export, and a transparent export leaves the Background out entirely.
- Put layers back together: Merge layers… under the stack opens a dialog that
  takes the layers you tick and the one you want them on. Marks arrive in the
  order they were painted, hidden layers come with their marks rather than
  losing them, locked layers stay out of it, and the Background can be merged
  onto but never away.
- Arrange that panel: a section heading drags the section into another order
  (out of the box: Image, Effects, Layers, Colour) — hold it first on a touch
  screen — and folds its section away. Settings → Panel switches a whole section
  off, or a single thing inside one — a page action, an effect by name, or one
  of the controls on the layer stack — and a section whose last row is switched
  off leaves the panel with it. Image and Start over inside it cannot be
  switched off; switching Layers off asks first and then merges every drawing
  down to a single unlocked Background layer. The arrangement travels with the
  settings file.
- Open on the same sheet every time: a page nobody has given a colour to is
  white and is drawn on in black, in a light app and a dark one alike, with the
  pen at its 0.5 mm liner in hand. All four answers are Settings → General →
  Defaults — the page colour, the ink, the tool and how that tool arrives set —
  and either colour can be set back to following the app theme. The two colours
  resolve as a page is painted, so changing one re-sheets or re-inks every
  drawing that never chose for itself and touches none that did; deleting the
  last drawing hands back a blank page with the same defaults on it.
- Keep several drawings, group them into folders, star the ones you return to,
  and archive the rest instead of deleting them.
- Tidy the sidebar with the gesture at hand: on touch, swipe a row right to
  archive it or left to bare a Delete button, and hold it to pick it up and drag
  it onto a folder, out to the top level, onto another sketchbook, or onto the
  archive — every target outlines itself as the row lifts. On a desktop the same
  actions live behind a right-click menu, and rows drag with the mouse.
- Keep several namespaces (separate sketchbooks), each with its own document,
  and move a drawing (or a whole folder, drawings and all) between them by
  dragging it onto another sketchbook's row. You start with one, called Default;
  the rest are made when you want them.
- Open the sidebar on a touch screen with an inward swipe from the edge it lives
  on, as well as from the header's hamburger. The canvas holds a touch that
  lands in that strip rather than drawing it, so the gesture leaves no mark.
- Drop an image file onto the canvas to add it to a drawing — move and scale it
  before settling it, and the page grows if the picture is bigger than the sheet
  — or onto the drawings list to start a new drawing named after the file.
- Undo and redo every mark; download a page as PNG, JPG or SVG, copy it to the
  clipboard, or export the whole document as JSON. Settings → Download chooses
  which types the menu offers, whether a file covers the whole page or crops to
  the marks, and whether the background is kept or transparent. A page made with
  no colour of its own downloads transparent as PNG or SVG whatever that setting
  says; JPG, which has no transparency, is given the colour the sheet would have
  had.
- Save a whole drawing as a `.pct` paint file and open it again exactly as it
  was. It is a zip holding one transparent PNG per layer plus a readable
  `manifest.json` — so other tools can read the layers — and the vector marks
  in `vectors.json` alongside, which is what makes reopening it lossless rather
  than a flatten. Open one from New image → Load, or by dropping it there.
- Work offline: it is an installable PWA with a precaching service worker.
- Optionally sync to a local folder, Dropbox, or Google Drive, with optional
  end-to-end encryption of the synced file.
- Press the header's disk button (or Ctrl/Cmd+S) to file the rendered layers out
  to that backend as browsable PNGs under `drawings/<name>-<tag>/`. Only that
  half of a save is manual: the marks push themselves on every settled edit, as
  they always have. A layer whose pixels have not changed costs nothing on the
  next press, because each layer's file name carries a hash of its content.

- Source: https://github.com/niclaslindstedt/paint
